- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
For centuries, cartographers had a problem that no one really has anymore: they kept running out of facts before they ran out of paper.

When you look at a sixteenth-century world map, the coastlines of Europe and the Mediterranean are rendered with fussy, obsessive precision—every harbor, every shoal, every jagged promontory accounted for. Then your eyes drift south or west, and the ink begins to loosen. Lines trail off into dotted guesses. Entire continents bulge like badly risen bread. And in the vast, empty corners of the sea, where the known world simply stopped, the mapmakers drew ships with billowing sails, compass roses, and occasionally a sea monster swallowing a vessel whole.

We like to repeat the phrase *Here be dragons*, though it almost never actually appeared on historical maps. What appeared more often was something quieter and, in its own way, stranger: *Terra Incognita*. Unknown land. Or worse, *phantom islands*—places that never existed at all, yet lingered on official nautical charts for hundreds of years.

There was Hy-Brasil, an island west of Ireland said to be cloaked in mist except for one day every seven years. There was Bermeja, off the coast of Mexico, which stayed on maps until the twentieth century before expeditions confirmed there was nothing there but empty water. Even as recently as 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed straight through Sandy Island in the Coral Sea—an island clearly marked on Google Earth and maritime charts—and found only a blue expanse four thousand feet deep. Someone in the nineteenth century had probably seen a floating raft of volcanic pumice, logged its coordinates, and for over a century, cartographers simply copied the mistake from one map to the next. Nobody wanted to be the person who deleted an island just in case it was still there.

It is easy to feel a little smug about this now. We live in the age of total cartography. Satellites sweep the globe in crisp, merciless passes, photographing the roof of your house, the shifting dunes of the Sahara, the exact contour of every rock in the Pacific. If you want to see a side street in Reykjavík or a dusty intersection in rural Argentina, you can drop a little yellow figure onto a screen and look around as if you were standing there. There are no accidental islands left. The paper is full.

And yet, I sometimes wonder if we misunderstand what happened to the blank spaces.

We tend to imagine mystery as something finite—a natural resource we mined until the vein ran dry. Once the last mountain is climbed and the last trench is pinged by sonar, wonder is supposed to pack its bags and leave.

But the unknown doesn’t actually vanish when you photograph it from orbit. It just changes scale.

Stand on a familiar street you have walked five hundred times, and try to remember what was in the storefront on the corner six years ago. Try to picture the exact cadence of a grandparent’s laugh, or the smell of your third-grade classroom after it rained. Suddenly, you are looking at a shoreline that dissolves into dotted lines. Our own memories are riddled with phantom islands—events we would swear happened, stitched together from a stray photograph and someone else’s retelling, sitting solid as granite on the map of our lives even though a closer look reveals only deep water.

The same is true of the people sitting across from us at dinner. You can know someone for twenty years, know how they take their coffee and which shoulder tightens up when they’re stressed, and still have no real map for the quiet interior weather they live inside every day. Every mind is mostly *terra incognita*. We send out small expeditions—a conversation late at night, an unguarded sentence in a car—and sketch a few miles of coastline before the fog rolls back in.

Even the physical world hasn’t surrendered as completely as a satellite view suggests. Most of the ocean floor is still mapped in coarser detail than the surface of Mars. Beneath a single square foot of forest soil, there are microscopic ecosystems we have barely named, let alone understood. The blank spaces didn’t disappear; they just moved down, and in, and out of sight.

There is a certain comfort in knowing where everything is. Nobody wants to steer a ship into an unmapped reef. Precision saves lives, gets groceries to the store, and brings planes down safely in the dark.

Still, I have a soft spot for those old mapmakers who refused to leave the margins entirely sterile—who looked at the edge of what they knew and responded not with boredom, or with a neat gray box labeled *No Data*, but with imagination. They understood something worth remembering: that the boundary of our knowledge isn’t a wall. It’s a coastline. And just past it, whether we draw them or not, the waters are still deep.

Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical reflective essay that uses the history of phantom islands to make uncertainty feel intimate rather than merely abstract.

## Grounded reading
The voice is assured and gently wonder-struck, moving from cartographic anecdotes into memory and the private lives of other people. Its pathos comes from the gap between wanting a complete map and accepting that people, places, and recollections remain partly unknowable. The reader is invited to see blankness not as a failure of knowledge but as a living edge where attention and imagination still matter.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds phantom islands, old maps, satellite imagery, imperfect memory, and the hidden interiors of people. It gives precision its practical value while resisting the idea that total measurement would eliminate wonder. The repeated coastline-and-unknown metaphor makes the essay’s central claim vivid: mystery changes scale rather than disappearing.

## Evidence line
> Every mind is mostly *terra incognita*.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay is coherent and stylistically distinctive, with a recurring metaphor that links geography to memory and human intimacy.
